name: Panama Canal
genZNote: The Panama Canal uses a system of locks to literally lift ships up and over land — it's basically an elevator for cargo ships.

sections.heading: 🚨 Location & What It Connects
bullets: An artificial, man-made canal across Panama in Central America, using a system of locks to raise and lower ships over the isthmus.
Connects the Atlantic Ocean (via the Caribbean Sea) to the Pacific Ocean.
Opened in 1914; operated by the Panama Canal Authority, an agency of the Panamanian government.

sections.heading: ⚓ Why It Matters
bullets: Removes the need to sail all the way around South America's Cape Horn to move between the Atlantic and Pacific.
Critical for trade between East Asia and the U.S. East Coast, and between Europe and the Americas' Pacific coast.

Its lock-based capacity is a real constraint — periods of low water levels in the canal's reservoirs have caused ship-transit restrictions in recent years, a good example of how a chokepoint's capacity itself can become a limiting factor.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: The Panama Canal is a man-made, lock-based canal across Panama connecting the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.
keyFacts: Man-made canal, opened 1914, located in Panama.
Connects Atlantic Ocean (via Caribbean Sea) to Pacific Ocean.
Uses a system of locks to lift ships over the isthmus.
Alternative route when unavailable: around South America's Cape Horn.
commonConfusion: Cape Horn (South America, alternative to Panama) is a different landmark from the Cape of Good Hope (Africa, alternative to Suez) — don't mix them up.

highYieldFacts: Panama Canal: man-made, opened 1914, uses locks, connects Atlantic ↔ Pacific.
Alternative when unavailable: Cape Horn route around South America.
Water-level constraints on its locks are a real, current capacity limitation.
commonTraps: Don't confuse the Panama Canal's lock system with a simple sea-level cut — ships are physically raised and lowered, unlike the Suez Canal which is sea-level.
mustRemember: Panama Canal = Central America's Atlantic-Pacific shortcut, lock-operated, man-made.
